L509@P11: Few cobayes receive mention in “La Tribu” – let alone this kind of mention! There
L510@P11: is no doubt about it; barely three years after the start of his studies, he was not only the
L511@P11: world’s premier specialist in his chosen domain, but he was already the mathematician he
L512@P11: ∗∗ The source of these remarks and much more fascinating detail is the article “Grothendieck and Banach Space Theory by J. Diestel in Alexandre Grothendieck: A Mathematical
L513@P11: Portrait, ed. L. Schneps, International Press, 2014. Diestel calls this approach, defining
L514@P11: classes of Banach spaces by properties of the operators acting on them “a first”.
L515@P11-12: 12was to become: Alexandre Grothendieck.
L516@P12: An end and a beginning: Fall 1952
L517@P12: By the time that Grothendieck had discovered the bulk of his results concerning
L518@P12: nuclear spaces, Schwartz and Dieudonn´e were convinced that, as a future mathematical
L519@P12: star, he needed a permanent position which would provide him with the best possible
L520@P12: working conditions as soon as possible.
L521@P12: A position in France was out of the question; the position “Attach´e de Recherche” at
L522@P12: the CNRS and the modest stipend it provided him was intended only as a sort of temporary
L523@P12: solution, a scholarship to support him through his doctoral degree, and unfortunately,
L524@P12: being stateless, he would have no access to a university position in France. The CNRS
L525@P12: had some flexibility, and they hoped to be able to negotiate something for him eventually,
L526@P12: but Grothendieck needed a job at once. Also, he needed to get away from Nancy.
L527@P12: As Godement explains it, “although Grothendieck was perfectly content there, he
L528@P12: realized very well that the intellectual level of the population wasn’t brilliant, and even the
L529@P12: mathematics department was hardly Harvard or Princeton. Not only that, but Paris wasn’t
L530@P12: any better than Nancy at that time. The only person really doing mathematics was Henri
L531@P12: Cartan.” In saying this, Godement wasn’t referring to the constellation of rising stars which
L532@P12: was very soon going to effect a fantastic and total reformation of French mathematics; he
L533@P12: was speaking of the older generation, those who could have been guides and mentors for
L534@P12: someone of Grothendieck’s capabilities. Brilliant as they were, Grothendieck had already
L535@P12: outgrown Dieudonn´e and Schwartz; he had mastered their work to the last comma, and
L536@P12: they, instead, were the ones poring over his new results. “Schwartz’s Fields Medal didn’t
L537@P12: impress him in the least. We all knew that Schwartz was a good mathematician, we
L538@P12: couldn’t care less about his medal,” says Godement, who was not unlike Grothendieck in
L539@P12: his complete disregard for social rank. “Anyway, even if Grothendieck had met Hilbert,
L540@P12: he’d just have said ‘How are you?’ He didn’t have any feeling of inferiority, even compared
L541@P12: to the greatest mathematicians ever. It was obvious that he already considered himself as
L542@P12: a very great mathematician. He was very sure of himself.”
L543@P12: The astounding mathematical growth he had undergone in Nancy, and the absolute
L544@P12: confidence that it gave him, is reflected in the snatches of his writing that can be found
L545@P12: from 1952. While his first letters to Dixmier cited above were formal and respectful, a
L546@P12: letter from May 1952 starts abruptly: “Cher Dixmier, Je n’ai jamais prouv´e ni pr´etendu
L547@P12: avoir prouv´e le th´eor`eme dont tu parles, et qui d’ailleurs est faux.”10 His impatience, his
L548@P12: annoyance at being misunderstood, and his complete lack of concern about appearing rude,
L549@P12: transpire clearly. A new side of his character was starting to show.
L550@P12: From the early fall, while Grothendieck was engaged in writing up the final version of
L551@P12: his thesis, Dieudonn´e and Schwartz were occupied in trying actively to obtain a position
L552@P12: for him in Brazil, a place where Schwartz had many close mathematical relations. It seems
L553@P12: that they first made an effort to find a position for him at the University of Rio de Janeiro,
L554@P12: where Paulo Ribenboim had returned already in July. A letter dated September 30, 1952
L555@P12: and signed by Dieudonn´e, Schwartz and C. Ehresmann, addressed to “Monsieur le Recteur
L556@P12: de l’Universidade do Brasil” (now UFRJ) recommends the creation of a second chair in
L557@P12-13: 13Analysis∗
L558@P13: . A letter from Dieudonn´e (now in Ann Arbor) to Grothendieck in October 1952
L559@P13: discusses the possibility of his spending the coming academic year in Princeton (chiefly
L560@P13: warning him of the serious difficulties he would be likely to face in trying to obtain a visa).
L561@P13: A letter from November discusses the possibility of publishing Grothendieck’s thesis as a
L562@P13: Memoir of the AMS, and commiserates with an apparent complaint about the inactivity of
L563@P13: the mathematical life in Nancy while Dieudonn´e, now on his way to Chicago, was roaming
L564@P13: about the Americas.
L565@P13: As a letter from January 1953 confirms, it was the University of S˜ao Paulo, where
L566@P13: Andr´e Weil (unwelcome in France after having avoided military service) had spent two years
L567@P13: in 1945-1947, and where Schwartz and Dieudonn´e also visited regularly, that ended up offering Grothendieck a two-year position for the academic years 1953 and 1954∗
L568@P13: . Dieudonn´e
L569@P13: advises him to submit an article to the journal Summa Brasiliensis, saying “Si vous partez
L570@P13: au Br´esil, il ne sera pas mauvais que vous ayiez un travail `a l’impression l`a-bas”,11 and
L571@P13: goes on to give him a clearly worded warning about difficulties that his forthright nature
L572@P13: might encounter in a foreign culture: “Si j’ai cru devoir vous mettre en garde en ce qui
L573@P13: concerne votre comportement vis-`a-vis des Br´esiliens, c’est que je connais tout de mˆeme
L574@P13: votre caract`ere entier et vos r´eactions `a certaines actions ou certaines gens; je ne trouve
L575@P13: pas du tout ¸ca antipathique, mais il faut que vous sachiez que l`a-bas la mentalit´e est telle
L576@P13: que lorsqu’on ne loue pas quelqu’un de fa¸con hyperbolique, c’est presque consid´er´e comme
L577@P13: une insulte!!”12 And, quoting Grothendieck as having accused him of being “seduced by
L578@P13: American gold”, Dieudonn´e ends tranquilly by observing that yes, he is no hero, but Americans are serious, honest and hard-working and he wouldn’t mind finding himself at the
L579@P13: same American university as Grothendieck some day.
L580@P13: By early 1953, then, Grothendieck was readying himself to leave Nancy for good
L581@P13: - though not without leaving a trace of himself behind. The Japanese mathematician
L582@P13: Reiji Takahashi∗∗, one of the first redactors of the Cartan seminar, arrived in Nancy very
L583@P13: shortly after Grothendieck had left, and found that his spirit was still present everywhere.
L584@P13: At a dance during a party at the home of Delsarte, the father of two charming daughters,
L585@P13: Takahashi noticed his host engaged in a heated discussion with a handsome young man in a
L586@P13: corner, ignoring both the girls and the assembled guests. Wondering what could be getting
L587@P13: them so excited, Takahashi joined them, only to hear Delsarte emitting sharp criticism of
L588@P13: the mathematical style of the mysterious Grothendieck, with a young Jean-Pierre Serre
L589@P13: ardently defending it. Weeks later, Takahashi entered a post office to mail a letter, and
L590@P13: the employee behind the window happened to notice that he was a mathematician. “So
L591@P13: you know Mr. Grothendieck?” enquired the employee with interest. Takahashi admitted
L592@P13: ∗ This information and much more was communicated to me by Alberto Azevedo, who
L593@P13: tried to discover all the details of Grothendieck’s visit to S˜ao Paulo, published an article
L594@P13: in Portuguese on the subject [ref] and patiently tried to answer the many questions I
L595@P13: addressed to him.
L596@P13: ∗ The academic year in Brazil runs from March to December, with January and February
L597@P13: being their summer vacation.
L598@P13: ∗∗ Hiroaki Nakamura was kind enough to contact Reiji Takahashi at my request, and have
L599@P13: a talk with him about Grothendieck, during which he noted down the amusing anecdotes
L600@P13: related here.
L601@P13-14: 14that he didn’t. “He was very strange,” he heard the employee murmur, before returning
L602@P14: to his other tasks.
L603@P14: What Grothendieck left behind him in Nancy went beyond mathematics and mathematicians. At some point during his stay there, on the last of his many searches for a
L604@P14: room to rent, he met Marcelle Driquert, moved into her house, and succumbed to what,
L605@P14: much later, he would call her “sex appeal”.
L606@P14: Marcelle Driquert (also called Aline), was an extremely unusual woman, of a type
L607@P14: calculated to appeal to Grothendieck’s sensitivities. For one, she was a good fourteen years
L608@P14: older than he was; not his mother’s age, certainly, but still an attractive “older woman” in
L609@P14: his eyes. For another, she was a real earth-mother, with a brood of four children ranging
L610@P14: in ages from 2 to 17 running around her house. And for a third, she was as much of a
L611@P14: social rebel as anyone that Grothendieck had ever met - an anarchist in lifestyle, if not
L612@P14: politically, as Grothendieck’s father Sascha had once described his mother Hanka, to her
L613@P14: pride. Marcelle worked as a shorthand-typist in a military tribunal, and rented out a room
L614@P14: in her house to make ends meet. Like Grothendieck himself, all of her children (apart
L615@P14: from Serge) bore their mother’s last name; all were from different fathers, and none of
L616@P14: those fathers were present. Marcelle loved children, but husbands were not part of her
L617@P14: life, as they had not been part of Hanka’s; her “I can do what I want” attitude was an
L618@P14: echo to Hanka’s oft-repeated “Ich kann machen, was ich will”. Hanka, apparently, did not
L619@P14: think much of Marcelle Driquert, which may not be very surprising - but after hearing
L620@P14: Grothendieck enthuse about her, the perspicacious Marie-H´el`ene Schwartz told her young
L621@P14: daughter: “He’s going to have a child with her”.
L622@P14: So during that last winter in Nancy, while Grothendieck was busy putting finishing
L623@P14: touches to his thesis, organizing the defence, submitting articles, and above all preparing
L624@P14: himself and his mother for the upcoming definitive move to Brazil, he lived at Marcelle’s
L625@P14: house; and in January 1953, she fell pregnant. It wasn’t a very good moment, just on
L626@P14: the eve of his departure, but Marcelle was not the type to calculate her own advantage.
L627@P14: She later told Serge, the son she bore to Grothendieck, that of all the men she had loved
L628@P14: in her life, Grothendieck was the only one who really counted; after him, there was never
L629@P14: anyone else. Serge was also given his father’s last name, which indicates that Grothendieck
L630@P14: officially recognized the child as his (a formality performed in the town hall). Marcelle
L631@P14: asked nothing from Grothendieck, and did nothing to try to prevent him from leaving.
L632@P14: She was aware that he had his mother to support and no source of income in France; in
L633@P14: any case he had no choice but to go. And she was used to raising children and earning her
L634@P14: living by herself.
L635@P14: When she said goodbye to Grothendieck, she was still in love with the young man of
L636@P14: whom she had seen only the very best side. She expected him to be interested in the child
L637@P14: he had fathered, if only from a distance, and to lend her a helping hand when he would be
